originalTitle: Coding agents in the social sciences
title: Coding agents in the social sciences
oneSentenceSummary: A survey of 1,260 social scientists reveals that while 81% have used AI chatbots, only 20% have adopted coding agents, with adoption sharply skewed by gender, career stage, and university prestige, and early users show more working papers but not more journal submissions.
summary: This research article from Anthropic presents findings from a survey of 1,260 quantitative social scientists fielded in early 2026, examining the adoption and impact of AI coding agents like Claude Code. The study finds that while 81% of respondents have used AI chatbots for research, only 20% regularly use coding agents. Adoption is highly uneven: economists (39%) and political scientists (25%) lead, while public health (6%) and education (4%) lag. Researchers with typically male names use coding agents at twice the rate of those with female names, and top university researchers are 40% more likely to adopt them. Coding agent users report starting more projects and posting more working papers and grant proposals, but not more journal submissions, suggesting productivity gains may be concentrated in early research stages. The authors caution these are descriptive, not causal, findings. Researchers are optimistic about AI boosting paper-writing productivity but less confident about positive effects on the broader field of social science.

mainPoints.point: Coding agent adoption among social scientists is low and highly uneven.
mainPoints.explanation: Only 20% of surveyed researchers use coding agents regularly, with adoption rates varying dramatically by discipline (39% in economics vs. 4% in education), career stage, gender, and university prestige.

mainPoints.point: Early adopters show increased output in early research stages but not in journal submissions.
mainPoints.explanation: Coding agent users post more working papers and grant proposals, but there is no evidence they submit more papers to journals, possibly due to the recent nature of adoption or tools being more useful for initial exploration than final polishing.

mainPoints.point: Researchers are more optimistic about AI's impact on individual productivity than on the field as a whole.
mainPoints.explanation: While 88% of respondents rate AI's potential to boost paper-writing productivity above 5 out of 10, 70% are more optimistic about personal productivity gains than about broader positive effects on social science, citing concerns about congestion and selective reporting.

mainPoints.point: The most common use of AI in social science research is for coding and editing, not writing.
mainPoints.explanation: 97% of coding agent users and 77% of other AI users employ AI to generate analysis code, followed by editing prose. Only a third have used AI to draft prose, countering the narrative that AI is primarily used for automated paper writing.

keyQuotes: The vast majority of respondents (81%) have tried using AI chatbots in research, particularly for writing code and editing prose. But only 20% have adopted coding agents---tools like Claude Code that autonomously write and execute analysis code---into their work.

There are sharp disparities in use of coding agents. Twice as many researchers with typically male names use coding agents as those with female names. Researchers at top universities are 40% more likely than others to use coding agents.
Coding agent users are starting more projects, posting more working papers, submitting more grants, and possibly sending out more conference submissions.
We find no evidence that coding agent users are submitting more new papers to journals or resubmitting papers more quickly.
Researchers are more optimistic about AI helping write publishable papers than about the effects of AI on the social sciences as a whole.
